passages.t: Azariah's word: if you seek him
passages.happening:
‘Now the Spirit of God came upon Azariah son of Oded’ (verse 1). He goes out to meet Asa: “Listen to me, Asa and all Judah and Benjamin. The LORD is with you when you are with Him. If you seek Him, He will be found by you, but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you” (verse 2).

He recalls a time when ‘Israel has been without the true God, without a priest to instruct them, and without the law’ (verse 3), ‘But in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought Him, and He was found by them’ (verse 4). In those days there was no safety for travelers, and nation was crushed by nation (verses 5-6). ‘But as for you, be strong; do not be discouraged, for your work will be rewarded’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 14 showed Asa seeking God in peace and relying on him in war. Here a prophet interprets the success and turns it into a lasting commitment. Victory could have made Asa proud, as strength made Rehoboam careless, but Azariah's word leads him deeper into reform.

Azariah son of Oded appears only here, one of several prophets in Chronicles not mentioned in Kings. His picture of Israel without the true God, without a teaching priest and without the law sounds most like the time of the judges, with its disorder and its repeated turning to God in distress. Some think he means the recent state of the northern kingdom, or speaks in words that fit any time of turning away.

The sermon is built on conditions: the LORD is with you when you are with him; seek him and he will be found, forsake him and he will forsake you. Found, matsa, is the promise of the chapter. The phrase he was found by them comes in the history lesson of verse 4 and again in verse 15, where it describes Judah's own experience, so the promise comes true within the chapter.
passages.later: Moses had said, ‘you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul’ (Deuteronomy 4:29). The book of Judges ends, ‘In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes’ (Judges 21:25).
passages.asks: The LORD is with you when you are with him. Ask where you have expected God's presence while walking away from him. And ask what it would mean, this week, to seek him in a way that lets him be found.

passages.t: A covenant sworn with all the heart
passages.happening:
Encouraged, Asa removes the idols from all Judah, Benjamin and the towns he had taken in Ephraim, and repairs the altar of the LORD (verse 8). People from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon come over to him in great numbers, ‘when they saw that the LORD his God was with him’ (verse 9). In the third month of his fifteenth year they gather in Jerusalem and offer sacrifices from the plunder (verses 10-11). ‘Then they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and soul’ (verse 12). Whoever would not seek the LORD was to be put to death (verse 13).

‘And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn it with all their heart. They had sought Him earnestly, and He was found by them. So the LORD gave them rest on every side’ (verse 15). Asa removes his grandmother Maacah as queen mother for making a detestable Asherah pole, and burns it in the Kidron Valley (verse 16). ‘The high places were not removed from Israel, but Asa’s heart was fully devoted all his days’ (verse 17). There is no more war until his thirty-fifth year (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
This is the high point of Asa's reign, and one of several covenant renewals in Chronicles, looking ahead to those under Jehoiada, Hezekiah and Josiah. The gathering took place in Asa's fifteenth year, about 896 BC. The third month was the time of the Feast of Weeks, and some see a link between the harvest festival and the oath. The sacrifices came from the plunder of chapter 14: the spoil of victory was given back to God. The ceremony follows ancient practice: assembly, sacrifice, a sworn oath, shevu'ah, and public joy with trumpets and rams' horns.

The northerners continue the movement begun in chapter 11. Simeon's land lay inside Judah's in the south, so its mention with northern tribes is a puzzle; it may reflect Simeonites tied to the north, or the Chronicler's concern to show all Israel gathering. The queen mother held real office at Judah's court, and deposing Maacah cost Asa in his own family. Kings calls her his mother; the Hebrew can mean grandmother, and she was Abijah's mother, so the BSB says grandmother. The rare word for her image, miphletset, means something horrifying. The Kidron Valley, between the city and the Mount of Olives, became the place where kings of Judah burned idols.

Verse 17 says the high places were not removed from Israel, while 14:3 says Asa removed them. The book sets the two side by side and does not explain them; readers reconcile them in more than one way.
passages.later: First Kings tells the same act: ‘He also removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole’ (1 Kings 15:13).
passages.hard:
Verse 13 says that anyone who would not seek the LORD should be put to death. How should this be understood?

The penalty follows the law of Deuteronomy, which required death for those in Israel who led others into, or practiced, the worship of other gods. In ancient Israel the covenant with God was also the nation's constitution, so turning away was treated as treason against the covenant community. Many interpreters also note that the clause works as the curse of the oath, the penalty the swearers called down on themselves, rather than a record of executions carried out.

Christians have generally held that this civil enforcement of worship belonged to Israel as a nation under the old covenant and is not a pattern for the church, which Jesus did not authorize to take up the sword. The history of Christians forcing belief is one the church has had to repent of. Readers still feel the severity of the verse, and it shows how seriously Israel took its covenant with God.
passages.asks: The people rejoiced over their oath because they had sworn it with all their heart. Ask what you have promised God half-heartedly. And ask whether there is anyone close to you, as Maacah was to Asa, whose influence you have been afraid to refuse.
